blocks.content: Most Docker networking problems fall into a small handful of recurring patterns, recognizing them quickly saves a lot of confused troubleshooting.
1. "I Can't Reach My Container"

This is almost always the Expose vs Publish confusion covered in the Docker Networking module, the first thing to check is whether the container was actually started with -p, an EXPOSE line in the Dockerfile alone changes nothing about reachability.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784481655933-149307127.png
blocks.alt: The first, most common check: was the port actually published?

blocks.content:
docker ps
# Check the PORTS column: does it show a mapping like 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp?
# If it's empty, the port was never published.

code.content:
docker ps
# Check the PORTS column: does it show a mapping like 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp?
# If it's empty, the port was never published.

codes.bash:
docker ps
# Check the PORTS column: does it show a mapping like 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp?
# If it's empty, the port was never published.

blocks.content: 2. "My Containers Can't Reach Each Other"

The next most common issue: two containers that should be able to talk are on different Docker networks, container-to-container communication (covered in its own topic) only works between containers sharing the same network, verify both are actually on the one you expect.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784481657440-146958944.png
blocks.alt: Check whether they're actually on the same network

blocks.content:
docker inspect web --format='{{.NetworkSettings.Networks}}'
docker inspect db --format='{{.NetworkSettings.Networks}}'
# Compare the network names, are they actually the same?

code.content:
docker inspect web --format='{{.NetworkSettings.Networks}}'
docker inspect db --format='{{.NetworkSettings.Networks}}'
# Compare the network names, are they actually the same?

codes.bash:
docker inspect web --format='{{.NetworkSettings.Networks}}'
docker inspect db --format='{{.NetworkSettings.Networks}}'
# Compare the network names, are they actually the same?

blocks.content: 3. "Name Resolution Isn't Working"

As covered in the DNS Resolution topic, automatic name-based resolution is a custom-network feature, if containers are still sitting on the default bridge network, resolving each other by name simply will not work, moving them to a custom network (or letting Compose create one automatically) is the fix.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784481658919-890717018.png
blocks.alt: Check whether you're still on the default bridge, which lacks this

blocks.content: 4. "Bind for 0.0.0.0:8080 Failed: Port Is Already Allocated"
blocks.text: 4. "Bind for 0.0.0.0:8080 Failed: Port Is Already Allocated"

blocks.content: This specific error means something else on the host, another container, or an entirely different process, is already using that host port. The fix is either stopping whatever is already using it, or simply choosing a different host port to publish to.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784481660757-83804945.png
blocks.alt: A host port collision, not a Docker bug

blocks.content:
lsof -i :8080
# Shows what's already using port 8080 on the host

code.content:
lsof -i :8080
# Shows what's already using port 8080 on the host

codes.bash:

# Shows what's already using port 8080 on the host

blocks.content: 5. The Tools That Actually Confirm What Is Happening
blocks.text: 5. The Tools That Actually Confirm What Is Happening

blocks.content: Beyond reasoning about it, docker network inspect shows exactly which containers are on a network and what IPs they have, and docker exec combined with curl or ping from inside a container lets you test connectivity directly from the container's own point of view, rather than guessing.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784481662456-673504992.png
blocks.alt: Confirm directly, rather than guessing from the outside

blocks.content:
docker network inspect mynet
docker exec app curl -v http://db:5432

code.content:
docker network inspect mynet
docker exec app curl -v http://db:5432

codes.bash:
docker network inspect mynet
docker exec app curl -v http://db:5432

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Most networking issues are one of a few recurring patterns: a missing -p, containers on different networks, the default bridge lacking DNS, or a host port collision.
docker network inspect and testing connectivity directly with docker exec + curl confirm what is actually happening instead of guessing.
